text: Some engagements explicitly test whether a defender notices and removes unauthorized persistence — a scheduled task, a service, a registry run key — placed to simulate what a real intrusion looks like days or weeks in. When that's part of the signed scope, it's treated exactly like any other test artifact: documented the moment it's created, time-stamped, and tied to the specific authorization that permits it. Persistence that isn't explicitly scoped is never something a tester improvises on their own judgment.

Every account, scheduled task, file, or configuration change made during an engagement goes into a running log the moment it's created, not reconstructed from memory at the end. That log is what makes cleanup possible and verifiable. It's also what protects the tester: if a client's own incident response team stumbles onto an unexplained artifact mid-engagement, that documented log is the proof it was authorized testing activity, not a real intrusion.

Before an engagement closes, a real cleanup checklist gets worked through: remove every test account created, remove any scheduled tasks or persistence mechanisms placed as scoped testing, restore any changed configuration to its original state, confirm no test tooling was left on disk, and cross-check all of it against the running documentation log, item by item, never from memory.

A completed cleanup isn't something a tester just does quietly. It's something the final report documents explicitly — what was created, when, and confirmation of removal. A client's security team needs that record to confirm their own environment is genuinely back to its pre-test state, and it closes the loop on the same chain-of-custody discipline this course opened with back in Lesson 1.

That closes out this chapter: from the judgment calls in Lesson 21, through the misconfiguration categories and detection signatures in Lessons 22 and 23, to the documentation discipline that proves everything was done responsibly. Chapter 7 picks up from here with purple team operations — putting you on the collaborative side of the exact detection signatures this chapter just covered.
